title: hscontrol: fix tag updates not propagating to node self view
body:
## Summary

When SetNodeTags changed a node's tags, the node's self view wasn't updated. The bug manifested as: the first SetNodeTags call updates the server but the client's self view doesn't update until a second call with the same tag.

Root cause: Three issues combined to prevent self-updates:

1. SetNodeTags returned PolicyChange which doesn't set OriginNode, so the mapper's self-update check failed.

2. The Change.Merge function didn't preserve OriginNode, so when changes were batched together, OriginNode was lost.

3. generateMapResponse checked OriginNode only in buildFromChange(), but PolicyChange uses RequiresRuntimePeerComputation which bypasses that code path entirely and calls policyChangeResponse() instead.

The fix addresses all three:
- state.go: Set OriginNode on the returned change
- change.go: Preserve OriginNode (and TargetNode) during merge
- batcher.go: Check OriginNode BEFORE RequiresRuntimePeerComputation

## Test plan

- [x] Add dedicated reproduction test `TestTagsIssue2978ReproTagReplacement` that validates the fix
- [x] Update 8 existing tests to verify node self view propagation after SetNodeTags
- [x] Add unit tests for Change.Merge preserving OriginNode/TargetNode

Fixes #2978

Fixes #3002 

## Summary

This PR adds a configurable way to derive the Headscale username from OIDC claims. It addresses IdPs (like Google) that do not emit `preferred_username`, enabling predictable, valid usernames without manual remediation.

## Changes

- Config: Introduce `oidc.username_claim_order` (array) that defines a priority list of claims to try.
  - Supported values: `preferred_username`, `email_localpart`, `email`, `name`, `sub`.
  - Default (when unset): `[preferred_username, email_localpart, email, name, sub]`.
- Username derivation helper: picks the first non-empty, syntactically valid candidate using existing `ValidateUsername` rules.
- OIDC flow: applies the mapping before creating/updating the user record so `Username()` resolves reliably.
- Documentation: added configuration reference and OIDC guide notes (including Google example).
- Tests: unit tests covering the derivation and common fallback cases.

## Example Configuration

```yaml
oidc:
  issuer: "https://accounts.google.com"
  client_id: "..."
  client_secret: "..."
  # Prefer preferred_username, otherwise use email local-part, then email
  username_claim_order:
    - preferred_username
    - email_localpart
    - email
```

## Notes

- Candidates are tried in order and must pass `ValidateUsername`.
- If the list is omitted, the default order is used.
- Default behavior preserves existing installs where `preferred_username` is present.
- No database migrations required.
- Username syntax is validated; all email verification and authorization constraints remain unchanged.

title: policy: fix asymmetric peer visibility with autogroup:self
body:
When autogroup:self was combined with other ACL rules (e.g., group:admin
-> *:*), tagged nodes became invisible to users who should have access.

The BuildPeerMap function had two code paths:
- Global filter path: used symmetric OR logic (if either can access, both
  see each other)
- Autogroup:self path: used asymmetric logic (only add peer if that
  specific direction has access)

This caused problems with one-way rules like admin -> tagged-server. The
admin could access the server, but since the server couldn't access the
admin, neither was added to the other's peer list.

Fix by using symmetric visibility in the autogroup:self path, matching
the global filter path behavior: if either node can access the other,
both should see each other as peers.

Credit to @vdovhanych for the analysis and proposed fix.

Fixes #2990

EXPERIMENT:

This PR contains a 9000~ line generated test file generated from having Claude agents run various ACL configuration against Tailscale SaaS and then observing the output Packet filters, and turn them into test cases.

Add extensive test coverage verifying Headscale's ACL policy behavior
matches Tailscale's coordination server. Tests cover:

- Source/destination resolution for users, groups, tags, hosts, IPs
- autogroup:member, autogroup:tagged, autogroup:self behavior
- Filter rule deduplication and merging semantics
- Multi-rule interaction patterns
- Error case validation

Key behavioral differences documented:
- Headscale creates separate filter entries per ACL rule; Tailscale
  merges rules with identical sources
- Headscale deduplicates Dsts within a rule; Tailscale does not
- Headscale does not validate autogroup:self source restrictions for
  ACL rules (only SSH rules); Tailscale rejects invalid sources

Tests are based on real Tailscale coordination server responses
captured from a test environment with 5 nodes (1 user-owned, 4 tagged).

title: policy/v2: accept RFC 3986 bracketed IPv6 in ACL destinations
body:
Headscale rejects IPv6 addresses with square brackets in ACL policy
destinations (e.g. `[fd7a:115c:a1e0::87e1]:80,443`), while Tailscale
SaaS accepts them.

The root cause is that `splitDestinationAndPort` uses
`strings.LastIndex(":")` which leaves brackets on the destination
string, and `netip.ParseAddr` does not accept brackets.

Add a bracket-handling branch at the top of `splitDestinationAndPort`
that uses `net.SplitHostPort` for RFC 3986 parsing when input starts
with `[`. The extracted host is validated with
`netip.ParseAddr`/`ParsePrefix` to ensure brackets are only accepted
around IP addresses and CIDR prefixes, not hostnames or other alias
types like tags and groups.

Fixes #2754

title: fix(policy/v2): use TrimPrefix for leading @ in username resolution
body:
## Summary

- Fix `Username.resolveUser` to strip the **leading** `@` from usernames using `TrimPrefix` instead of `TrimSuffix`
- The ACL policy format uses `@username` (leading `@`), but `TrimSuffix` only strips a trailing `@`, so no group member usernames ever matched, causing all group-based ACL rules to silently compile to empty filter sets

## Root Cause

```go
// Before (bug): trailing @ stripped, but policy uses leading @
uTrimmed := strings.TrimSuffix(u.String(), "@")
// "@laronica.lawson" → "@laronica.lawson" (unchanged, never matches)

// After (fix): strip both leading and trailing @
uTrimmed := strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSuffix(u.String(), "@"), "@")
// "@laronica.lawson" → "laronica.lawson" (matches user.Name)
```

## Impact

This bug caused:
- All group-based ACL source rules to produce empty IP sets (silently skipped)
- `/debug/filter` returning `null` when only group-based rules exist
- `ReduceRoutes` and `BuildPeerMap` seeing no matchers, so subnet routes were never distributed to group members
- The `src: *` workaround bypassed the bug because wildcard sources don't go through `resolveUser`

## Verification

Tested on a live headscale v0.27.1 deployment with:
- A subnet router advertising `10.0.0.0/8` and a 4via6 prefix
- Group-based ACLs (`group:n8n → n8n-svc:5678`)
- Before fix: `/debug/filter` = `null`, router not visible in peer netmap
- After fix: filter rules correctly compiled, router visible with scoped routes, end-to-end connectivity confirmed

All existing policy tests pass.

Fixes #3104

title: fix: OIDC expiry 0 sets nil instead of far-future date
body:
Fixes #3111

## Problem

When `oidc.expiry` is set to `0` (meaning "no expiry"), headscale sets the node expiry to `MaxDuration` (~292 years in the future). This results in a far-future date like `2318-06-08` in the database instead of NULL. Clients like Headplane cannot distinguish this from a real expiry and fail to show the "no expiry" tag.

## Fix

Three changes:

1. **`hscontrol/oidc.go` - `determineNodeExpiry`**: When `Expiry` equals `MaxDuration`, return zero time instead of adding 292 years to now.

2. **`hscontrol/oidc.go` - `handleRegistration`**: When the computed expiry is zero time, pass `nil` (instead of `&expiry`) to `HandleNodeFromAuthPath`, resulting in NULL in the database. This is consistent with how `IsExpired()` already treats nil expiry as "not expired".

3. **`hscontrol/types/config.go`**: Exported `MaxDuration` so it can be referenced from the `hscontrol` package.

## Test

Added `TestDetermineNodeExpiry` with three test cases:
- `zero_expiry_means_no_expiry`: verifies MaxDuration config returns zero time (fails without fix: returns year 2318)
- `normal_expiry_returns_future_time`: verifies normal expiry still works
- `use_token_expiry`: verifies UseExpiryFromToken still works

Tested locally on macOS ARM (Apple Silicon). All hscontrol tests pass.

title: policy: add App Connector support via nodeAttrs
body:
App connector configuration is now delivered through the `nodeAttrs` `app` field, the way Tailscale delivers it, instead of the custom `appConnectors` policy block this PR originally added. Rebased on current main.

Following up on @Matchlighter's suggestion: after #3251 landed nodeAttrs, the only missing piece was valued capabilities. `nodeAttrs` carried key-only caps through `attr` and nothing else.

## What changed

1. `NodeAttrGrant` gets an `app` field (`tailcfg.NodeCapMap`), stamped into the node's CapMap in `compileNodeAttrs` next to the key-only attrs. Payloads are passed through opaquely and the client interprets them.
2. App connectors ride that generic path, so there is no app-connector-specific code left anywhere: `compileNodeAttrs` -> `NodeCapMap` -> `NodesWithChangedCapMap` -> `SelfUpdate`.
3. The `PolicyChange{IncludeSelf: true}` broadcast the first version needed is gone. A reload now sends a targeted self update only to nodes whose config actually changed, which also fixes the reload propagation @dmeremyanin hit.
4. Removed: the `appConnectors` block, the `AppConnector` / `AppConnectorAttr` types, `AppConnectorConfigForNode` and its wrappers, the `builder.go` injection, and the load-time domain validation.

```json
{
  "tagOwners": {
    "tag:connector": ["admin@"]
  },
  "nodeAttrs": [
    {
      "target": ["tag:connector"],
      "app": {
        "tailscale.com/app-connectors": [
          {
            "name": "Internal Apps",
            "connectors": ["tag:connector"],
            "domains": ["internal.example.com", "*.corp.example.com"],
            "routes": ["10.0.0.0/8"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## What works and what does not

Works today: the capability reaches every node the `target` selects, hardcoded `routes` are advertised as soon as the connector gets its config, and policy reloads propagate.

Does not work yet: Headscale does not tell clients to send DNS queries for the configured domains to the connector, so dynamic domain discovery does not happen on its own. That is the DNS side of the feature and it belongs with the v0.31 work. `docs/ref/policy.md` says so in a warning admonition, `features.md` marks App Connectors unchecked with the delivery part checked underneath, so nobody reads this as done.

Two deliberate behavior notes:

1. The cap ships on `target` match regardless of `tailscale set --advertise-connector`. This matches Tailscale, where the client gates on its local connector flag and on the payload's `connectors` field.
2. No load-time domain validation. Payloads are pass through, so a malformed domain surfaces client side.

## Cap name validation

Grant `app` cap names go through `validateCapabilityName`, which rejects URL-formatted names and `tailscale.com/*` names that are not in `tailscaleCapAllowlist`. The `app` field on nodeAttrs needs the same guard, otherwise a policy can ship any `tailscale.com` capability to a node with nothing behind it:

```json
{ "target": ["*"], "app": { "tailscale.com/cap/funnel": [] } }
```

So there is a `validateNodeCapabilityName` with its own allowlist, currently holding only `tailscale.com/app-connectors`. It is a separate map because `tailscaleCapAllowlist` is keyed by `tailcfg.PeerCapability` and its comment is about peer caps. Names in an operator's own domain, like `example.com/app/my-cap`, still pass through. The reasoning is the one already in `nodeAttrUnsupportedCaps`: rejecting at load beats letting a node advertise something that does not work.

If you would rather have one shared allowlist, or no gate at all on the nodeAttrs side, say so and I will change it.

## Tests

Unit (`hscontrol/policy/v2/appconnector_test.go`), on the shared nodeAttrs fixtures:

1. `TestAppConnectorViaNodeAttrs`: targeted node gets both configs, non-targeted nodes get nothing, `routes` round trips through `appctype.AppConnectorAttr`.
2. `TestAppConnectorWildcardTarget`: `*` reaches every node.
3. `TestAppConnectorChangeTracking`: the cap participates in `NodesWithChangedCapMap`, which is what makes the `IncludeSelf` removal safe.
4. `TestValidateNodeCapabilityName` and `TestAppConnectorUnsupportedCapRejected`: the allowlist, both at the helper and at policy load.

Integration (`integration/appconnector_test.go`): `TestAppConnectorBasic`, `TestAppConnectorNonMatchingTag`, `TestAppConnectorWildcardConnector`. Configs are marshalled through `appctype.AppConnectorAttr` so the tests use the same wire shape a Tailscale hosted control plane emits.

title: Add prominent warning banner for non-standard IP prefixes
body:
Closes #3055
Closes #3062

## Summary

- Adds a reusable `warnBanner()` function that prints a large ASCII-art "Warning!" banner to the log output, matching the format from #3055
- Modifies `prefixV4()` and `prefixV6()` to return a boolean indicating whether the configured prefix is outside the standard range, instead of logging independently
- Consolidates the check in `LoadServerConfig()` so the banner fires **once** even if both prefixes are non-standard
- Updates `config-example.yaml` to clarify that subsets of the default ranges are fine, but ranges outside CGNAT/ULA are not

## What the warning looks like

When a user configures a prefix outside the standard CGNAT or ULA range, they'll see something like this at startup:

```
################################################################
###      __          __              _             _         ###
###      \ \        / /             (_)           | |        ###
###       \ \  /\  / /_ _ _ __ _ __  _ _ __   __ _| |        ###
###        \ \/  \/ / _` | '__| '_ \| | '_ \ / _` | |        ###
###         \  /\  / (_| | |  | | | | | | | | (_| |_|        ###
###          \/  \/ \__,_|_|  |_| |_|_|_| |_|\__, (_)        ###
###                                           __/ |          ###
###                                          |___/           ###
################################################################
###                                                          ###
###  You have overridden the default Headscale IP prefixes   ###
###  with a range outside of the standard CGNAT and/or ULA   ###
###  ranges. This is NOT a supported configuration.          ###
###                                                          ###
###  Using subsets of the default ranges (100.64.0.0/10 for  ###
###  IPv4, fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48 for IPv6) is fine. Using      ###
###  ranges outside of these will cause undefined behaviour   ###
###  as the Tailscale client is NOT designed to operate on    ###
###  any other ranges.                                        ###
###                                                          ###
###  Please revert your prefixes to subsets of the standard  ###
###  ranges as described in the example configuration.        ###
###                                                          ###
###  Any issue raised using a range outside of the supported ###
###  range will be labelled as wontfix and closed.            ###
###                                                          ###
################################################################
```

## Design decisions

- **`warnBanner()` is reusable** — takes `[]string` lines and formats them into the banner box, so it can be used for other critical warnings in the future
- **Warning fires once** — even if both v4 and v6 are non-standard, only one banner is printed (per review feedback on #3062)
- **Subsets are fine** — the check uses `ContainsPrefix` which correctly allows subsets like `100.64.0.0/24` within the CGNAT range

- [x] Subset of standard range (e.g., 100.64.0.0/24) → no warning
- [x] Non-standard prefix (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) → warning banner printed
- [x] Both prefixes non-standard → single warning banner

title: fix: persist empty ApprovedRoutes and Endpoints to database
body:
## Summary

Fixes #3110

When an admin rejects all routes for a node (`headscale nodes approve-routes -i 5 -r ""`), the empty `ApprovedRoutes` slice is correctly set in the in-memory NodeStore but never written to the database. On restart, the old routes reappear.

**Root cause**: `persistNodeToDB` uses GORM's `.Updates(struct)`, which silently skips zero-value fields. An empty `[]netip.Prefix` is a zero value, so it's dropped.

**Fix**: After the `.Updates()` call in `persistNodeToDB`, explicitly persist empty `ApprovedRoutes` and `Endpoints` slices by writing `"[]"` — the same pattern already used in `db.SetApprovedRoutes` (node.go:242-244).

This is done in `persistNodeToDB` rather than individual callers so it fixes the issue for all code paths, and also addresses a latent bug where `Endpoints` could similarly fail to persist when empty.

title: mapper/batcher: replace connected map with per-node disconnectedAt
body:
The Batcher's connected field used *time.Time pointer semantics to encode three states: nil meant connected, non-nil meant disconnected-at-timestamp, and key-missing meant never-seen. This was easy to misread (nil meaning "connected" inverts typical Go idioms), redundant with the nodes map that already tracks active connections, and required keeping two parallel concurrent maps in sync. It also contained a bug where RemoveNode used new(time.Now()) instead of &now, producing a zero-valued timestamp.

This replaces the separate connected map with a disconnectedAt atomic.Pointer[time.Time] field directly on multiChannelNodeConn, the object that already manages each node's connections. IsConnected drops from two map lookups to one, ConnectedMap and Debug iterate a single map instead of two, and cleanupOfflineNodes scans b.nodes directly. The markDisconnectedIfNoConns helper is removed.

title: mapper/batcher: serialize per-node work to prevent out-of-order delivery
body:
processBatchedChanges queued each pending change for a node as a separate work item. Since multiple workers pull from the same channel, two changes for the same node could be processed concurrently by different workers. This caused out-of-order MapResponse delivery and a data race between updateSentPeers (Clear+Store) and computePeerDiff (Range) on the shared lastSentPeers map.

This change bundles all pending changes for a node into a single work item so one worker processes them sequentially. A per-node workMu mutex serializes processing across consecutive batch ticks, preventing a second worker from starting on the next tick's bundle while the current one is still in progress. Inter-node parallelism is preserved — different nodes are still processed concurrently by different workers.

Fixes #3140

title: Fix list-routes -i flag not filtering by node ID under approve-routes
body:
## Summary

Fixes the `-i` flag being ignored when running `headscale nodes approve-routes list-routes -i <id>`, which returned routes for all nodes instead of the specified one.

## Problem

`list-routes` was registered only as a direct subcommand of `nodes`, not `approve-routes`. Running `headscale nodes approve-routes list-routes -i 12` caused cobra to parse `-i` as belonging to `approve-routes` rather than `list-routes`, so `list-routes` saw `identifier=0` and returned all nodes.

## Fix

- Changed `approve-routes` `-i` flag from `Flags()` to `PersistentFlags()` so subcommands inherit it
- Registered `list-routes` as a subcommand of `approve-routes`
- `list-routes` remains accessible directly via `headscale nodes list-routes -i <id>` for backward compatibility

Both command paths now work correctly:
- `headscale nodes list-routes -i 12`
- `headscale nodes approve-routes list-routes -i 12`

## Summary

`DestroyUser` in `hscontrol/db/users.go` calls `ListPreAuthKeys(tx)` which returns **all** pre-auth keys in the database, then deletes every one of them. This means deleting any single user wipes all pre-auth keys for the entire system.
